title: Rambour: grace raised Adam's natural gifts, making him a son and heir, not only a faithful servant
source_text: XXXVIII. Ramburtius similiter in Adamo agnoscit dona supernaturalia, thesi vigesima nona modo citatae disputationis. Neque propterea, inquit, dona supernaturalia ab Adamo removemus. Gratia enim Dei haec eadem dona naturalia exornabat, in dies attollebat: quemadmodum gratia non destruit naturam, sed eam dirigit, & altius quam quo per vires suas eniti potest erigit. Ideo primus homo non modo fuit eximia creatura, sed etiam filius Dei, assumptus ad cernendam haereditatem caelestem, id est, non tantum habuit per naturam rationem servi fidelis, Domini voluntatem probe intelligentis, eamque perfecte exequentis, sed etiam per gratiam dignitatem filii paternam benedictionem & haereditatem sperantis.
pass_a_gloss: Rambour similarly acknowledges in Adam supernatural gifts, in thesis twenty-nine of the disputation just cited. Nor on that account, he says, do we remove supernatural gifts from Adam. For the grace of God adorned these same natural gifts, raised them daily: just as grace does not destroy nature, but directs it, and raises it higher than it can strive by its own powers. Therefore the first man was not only an excellent creature, but also a son of God, taken up to receive the heavenly inheritance, that is, he had not only by nature the condition of a faithful servant, understanding well the will of the Lord, and carrying it out perfectly, but also by grace the dignity of a son hoping for the paternal blessing and inheritance.
pass_b_english: Rambour likewise recognizes supernatural gifts in Adam, in thesis 29 of the disputation just cited: "This does not mean that we take supernatural gifts away from Adam. God's grace adorned these same natural gifts and lifted them higher day by day, just as grace does not destroy nature but directs it and raises it higher than it can climb by its own strength.

"So the first man was not only an outstanding creature but also a son of God, adopted to enter into the heavenly inheritance. By nature he had the standing of a faithful servant who understood his Lord's will well and carried it out perfectly; by grace he also had the dignity of a son who hoped for his Father's blessing and inheritance."

choices.why: Cernere hereditatem is the Roman legal formula for formally accepting an inheritance.
